title: Chapter 3 — The Spouter-Inn
paragraphs: Entering the gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, rambling entryway with old-fashioned wood paneling that reminded you of the bulkheads of some condemned old ship. On one side hung a very large oil painting, so thoroughly covered in soot and grime that you could only figure out what it depicted through careful study, repeated visits, and asking the neighbors. Such unfathomable masses of shadow that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the days of the New England witch trials, had tried to paint chaos itself under a spell. But through much earnest contemplation and a great deal of pondering — and especially by throwing open the little back window to let in more light — you finally concluded that such an interpretation, however wild, might not be completely off the mark.

But what puzzled you most was a long, dark, ominous mass of something hovering in the center of the painting, above three blue, dim, vertical lines floating in a nameless froth. A boggy, soggy, squelchy picture — enough to drive a nervous person crazy. Yet there was something almost sublime about it that froze you in place until you swore to yourself you'd figure out what it meant. Bright ideas would flash through you: It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale. It's the four primal elements at war. It's a blasted heath. It's an Arctic winter scene. It's the breaking up of the frozen river of Time. But eventually all these theories gave way to that one ominous something in the center. Once you figured that out, everything else fell into place. But wait — doesn't it look faintly like a gigantic fish? The great Leviathan himself?

In fact, the artist's intention seemed to be this (my own theory, partly based on the combined opinions of many old-timers I'd consulted): the painting shows a ship rounding Cape Horn in a massive hurricane. The half-sunk vessel is wallowing in the waves with its three broken masts barely visible, and a furious whale, trying to leap clean over the ship, is in the act of impaling itself on all three mastheads.

The opposite wall was covered with a barbaric display of monstrous clubs and spears. Some were studded with glittering teeth like ivory saws; others were tufted with knots of human hair; one was sickle-shaped, with a huge sweeping handle like the arc a long-armed mower cuts through fresh grass. You shuddered as you looked, wondering what monstrous cannibal could have gone harvesting death with such a terrifying weapon. Mixed in were rusty old whaling lances and harpoons, all broken and bent. Some had stories behind them. With this lance, now wildly twisted, Nathan Swain had killed fifteen whales between sunrise and sunset fifty years ago. And that harpoon — now bent like a corkscrew — was thrown in the Java seas and run off with by a whale, which was killed years later off the Cape of Blanco. The original iron had entered near the tail and, like a restless needle traveling through a human body, migrated forty feet before lodging in the hump.

Crossing the dusky entry and passing through a low archway — cut through what must once have been a great central chimney — you entered the public room. An even darker place, with such heavy low beams above and such worn, wrinkled planks below that you'd almost think you were treading the decks of some ancient ship, especially on a howling night when the old building rocked like an anchored ark. On one side stood a long, low, shelf-like table covered with cracked glass cases full of dusty curiosities gathered from the world's most remote corners. Projecting from the far corner was a dark den — the bar — a crude imitation of a right whale's head. Whatever the intention, there stood the vast arched jawbone of a whale, so wide a coach could nearly drive beneath it. Inside were shabby shelves with old bottles, decanters, and flasks; and within those jaws of destruction, like another cursed Jonah (which was indeed his nickname), a little withered old man hustled about, selling the sailors delirium and death for their money.

Terrible were the glasses he served his poison in. Though perfectly cylindrical on the outside, the villainous green tumblers tapered deceptively on the inside to a cheating bottom. Lines were crudely etched into the glass like latitude markings. Fill to this line and it costs a penny; to this line, a penny more; all the way up to the full glass — the Cape Horn measure — which you could gulp down for a shilling.

When I entered, I found several young seamen gathered around a table, examining by dim light various specimens of scrimshaw. I found the landlord and told him I wanted a room. He said his house was full — not a bed available. 'But hold on,' he added, tapping his forehead, 'you wouldn't mind sharing a harpooneer's blanket, would you? I expect you're going whaling, so you'd better get used to that sort of thing.'

I told him I never liked sleeping two to a bed; that whether I'd agree would depend on who the harpooneer was; and that if there really was no other option, and the harpooneer wasn't too objectionable, then rather than wander any further through a strange town on such a bitter night, I'd put up with sharing any decent man's blanket.
'Thought so. All right, have a seat. Supper? You want supper? It'll be ready shortly.'

I sat down on an old wooden bench carved all over like a seat on the Battery. At one end, a ruminative sailor was further decorating it with his jackknife, stooping over and working diligently at the space between his knees. He was attempting a ship under full sail, but he wasn't making much progress.

At last four or five of us were called to eat in an adjoining room. It was cold as Iceland — no fire at all; the landlord said he couldn't afford it. Nothing but two gloomy tallow candles, each in a paper sleeve. We had to button up our jackets and hold our cups of scalding tea with half-frozen fingers. But the food was substantial — not just meat and potatoes but dumplings. Good heavens, dumplings for supper! One young fellow in a green coat attacked those dumplings in a most alarming manner.
'My boy,' said the landlord, 'you're going to have nightmares for sure.'
'Landlord,' I whispered, 'that's not the harpooneer, is it?'
'Oh no,' he said, with a sort of diabolically amused look, 'the harpooneer is a dark-complexioned fellow. He never eats dumplings — nothing but steaks, and he likes them rare.'
'The devil he does,' I said. 'Where is this harpooneer? Is he here?'
'He'll be here before long,' was the answer.
I couldn't help it — I was starting to feel suspicious of this 'dark-complexioned' harpooneer. At the very least, I resolved that if we were to share a bed, he'd have to undress and get in before me.
After supper, the company returned to the bar room. Having nothing else to do, I decided to spend the rest of the evening as a spectator.

Soon a riotous noise was heard from outside. Jumping up, the landlord cried, 'That's the Grampus's crew! I saw her reported offshore this morning — three-year voyage, full ship. Hurrah, boys! Now we'll have the latest news from the Fiji Islands!'

The tramping of sea boots echoed in the entry; the door burst open, and in rolled a wild set of sailors. Wrapped in shaggy watch coats, heads muffled in wool scarves, all patched and ragged, beards stiff with icicles, they looked like an eruption of bears from Labrador. They'd just come from their boat, and this was the first building they'd entered. No wonder they made straight for the whale's mouth — the bar — where the wrinkled little old Jonah poured them full glasses all around. One complained of a bad cold, so Jonah mixed him a tar-like brew of gin and molasses, swearing it was a guaranteed cure for all colds whatsoever, no matter how long-standing or where they'd been caught.
The liquor quickly went to their heads, as it usually does with even the heaviest drinkers who've just come ashore, and they began leaping about wildly.

I noticed, however, that one of them held somewhat apart. Though he clearly didn't want to dampen his shipmates' fun with his own sober expression, he mostly refrained from joining the noise. This man interested me at once. Since fate had decreed he'd soon become my shipmate — though only a sleeping partner, as far as this story goes — I'll describe him briefly. He stood a full six feet tall, with noble shoulders and a chest like a vault. I've rarely seen such powerful build in a man. His face was deeply tanned, making his white teeth dazzle by contrast, and in the depths of his eyes floated memories that didn't seem to bring him much joy. His voice marked him as a Southerner, and from his fine build I guessed he must be one of those tall mountaineers from Virginia's Allegheny Ridge. When his companions' revelry reached its peak, this man slipped away unnoticed. I didn't see him again until he became my comrade at sea. Within minutes, though, his shipmates missed him, and being apparently a great favorite, they raised a cry of 'Bulkington! Bulkington! Where's Bulkington?' and rushed out in pursuit.

It was now about nine o'clock. The room felt almost supernaturally quiet after the commotion, and I began congratulating myself on a little plan that had occurred to me just before the sailors arrived.

Nobody prefers to sleep two in a bed. In fact, you'd rather not share one even with your own brother. People like privacy when they sleep. And when it comes to sharing a bed with a complete stranger, in a strange inn, in a strange town — and that stranger a harpooneer — your objections multiply enormously. And there was no reason I, as a sailor, should be any more willing than anyone else. Sailors don't share beds at sea any more than bachelor kings do on land. True, they all sleep in one room, but each man has his own hammock, his own blanket, and sleeps in his own skin.

The more I thought about this harpooneer, the less I wanted to share a bed with him. Being a harpooneer, his clothes were probably not the tidiest. I began fidgeting all over. Besides, it was getting late, and my supposedly decent harpooneer should have been home and heading to bed by now. What if he stumbled in at midnight — what nasty dive might he be coming from?
'Landlord! I've changed my mind about the harpooneer. I won't sleep with him. I'll try this bench.'

'Suit yourself. Sorry I can't spare you a tablecloth for a mattress — this is a rough board,' he said, feeling the knots and notches. 'But wait, Scrimshander — I've got a carpenter's plane behind the bar. Hold on, I'll make you nice and comfortable.' With that he produced the plane, dusted the bench with his old silk handkerchief, and set to planing away at my bed, grinning like an ape. Shavings flew everywhere until the blade hit an indestructible knot. He nearly sprained his wrist. I told him for heaven's sake to stop — the bed was soft enough, and all the planing in the world couldn't turn a pine plank into a featherbed. So, gathering the shavings with another grin and tossing them into the big stove, he went about his business and left me to my thoughts.

I now took the measure of the bench, and found that it was a foot too short — but that could be remedied with a chair. It was also a foot too narrow, and the other bench in the room was about four inches higher than the planed one, so there was no yoking them together. I then placed the first bench lengthwise along the only clear space against the wall, leaving a little interval between it and the wall for my back to settle down in. But I soon found that such a draft of cold air came over me from under the sill of the window that this plan would never do at all, especially as another current from the rickety door met the one from the window, and the two together formed a series of small whirlwinds in the immediate vicinity of the very spot where I had thought to spend the night.

To hell with that harpooneer, I thought. But wait — couldn't I sneak into his room, bolt the door from inside, and jump into his bed, too soundly asleep to be roused by even the loudest knocking? It wasn't a bad idea, but on second thought I dropped it. Who knew but the next morning, the moment I stepped out, the harpooneer might be standing in the hallway, ready to knock me down!

Still, looking around and seeing no possible way to spend a bearable night except in someone else's bed, I began to think I might be harboring unwarranted prejudice against this unknown harpooneer. I'll wait a while, I thought. He must be showing up soon. I'll get a good look at him, and maybe we'll become perfectly good bedfellows after all — you never know.
But though the other boarders kept arriving one by one and going to bed, there was no sign of my harpooneer.
'Landlord!' I said. 'What sort of fellow is he — does he always keep such late hours?' It was now nearly midnight.

The landlord chuckled with his dry chuckle, looking mightily amused about something beyond my understanding. 'No,' he answered, 'usually he's an early bird — early to bed and early to rise. But tonight he went out peddling, you see, and I can't imagine what's keeping him so late, unless maybe he can't sell his head.'

'Can't sell his head? What kind of crazy story is this?' I said, getting furious. 'Do you mean to tell me, landlord, that this harpooneer is actually out this Saturday night — or rather Sunday morning — peddling his head around town?'
'That's exactly it,' said the landlord, 'and I told him he couldn't sell it here. The market's overstocked.'
'Overstocked with what?' I shouted.
'With heads, of course. Aren't there too many heads in the world?'
'Look here, landlord,' I said, quite calmly, 'you'd better stop spinning that yarn. I wasn't born yesterday.'
'Maybe not,' he said, pulling out a stick and whittling a toothpick, 'but I think you'll be done brown if that harpooneer hears you slandering his head.'
'I'll break it for him,' I said, flying into a rage again at the landlord's incomprehensible nonsense.
'It's already broken,' he said.
'Broken?' I said. 'Broken, you mean?'
'Yep, and that's the very reason he can't sell it, I guess.'

'Landlord,' I said, walking up to him cool as a glacier in a blizzard, 'landlord, stop whittling. You and I need to come to an understanding, and right now. I come to your house wanting a bed; you tell me you can only give me half of one, the other half belonging to some harpooneer. And about this harpooneer, whom I haven't seen, you keep telling me the most mystifying, infuriating stories, designed to make me deeply uncomfortable about the man you're assigning as my bedfellow — an arrangement, landlord, which is among the most intimate known to man. I now demand that you speak plainly and tell me who and what this harpooneer is, and whether I'll be safe spending the night with him. And first, please retract that story about selling his head — because if it's true, that's strong evidence the man is stark mad, and I have no intention of sleeping with a madman. And you, sir — you, landlord — by knowingly trying to make me do so, you'd be making yourself liable for criminal prosecution.'

'Well,' said the landlord, drawing a long breath, 'that's a mighty long speech for a fellow who swears a little now and then. But take it easy — this harpooneer I've been telling you about just arrived from the South Seas, where he bought up a batch of embalmed New Zealand heads — great curiosities, you know — and he's sold all of them except one, which he's trying to sell tonight because tomorrow is Sunday, and it wouldn't do to be selling human heads on the streets when people are going to church. He wanted to last Sunday, but I stopped him just as he was heading out the door with four heads strung together like a string of onions.'

This explanation cleared up the mystery and showed the landlord hadn't been trying to fool me. But still — what was I to think of a harpooneer who stayed out on a Saturday night deep into the Sabbath, engaged in the cannibal business of selling dead men's heads?
'Mark my words, landlord — that harpooneer is a dangerous man.'

'He pays regular,' was the reply. 'But come, it's getting terribly late. You'd better turn in — it's a nice bed. My wife Sal and I slept in it the night we were married. There's plenty of room for two; it's an enormous bed. Before we gave it up, Sal used to put little Sam and Johnny at the foot of it. But one night I went thrashing around in my sleep and poor Sam got thrown on the floor and nearly broke his arm. After that, Sal said it wouldn't do. Come along, I'll give you a light.' He lit a candle and held it toward me, offering to lead the way. But I stood undecided. Then, glancing at a clock in the corner, he exclaimed, 'By George, it's Sunday! You won't see that harpooneer tonight — he must have anchored somewhere. Come along, then — come on, won't you?'
I thought it over for a moment, then upstairs we went. I was shown into a small room, cold as a clam, furnished with an enormous bed — big enough for four harpooneers to sleep side by side.

'There,' said the landlord, setting the candle on a battered old sea chest that doubled as a washstand and table. 'Make yourself comfortable. Good night.' I turned from examining the bed, but he'd already vanished.

Folding back the bedspread, I leaned over and inspected the bed. Not the most elegant, but it passed muster. I glanced around the room: besides the bed and the chest, the only furniture was a crude shelf, the four bare walls, and a wallpapered fireboard showing a man harpooning a whale. The room also contained a hammock rolled up in one corner, a large sailor's bag — the harpooneer's wardrobe, no doubt, serving as a suitcase — some strange bone fishhooks on the shelf above the fireplace, and a tall harpoon standing at the head of the bed.

But what was this on the chest? I picked it up, held it to the light, felt it, smelled it, and tried every possible way to figure out what it was. The closest comparison I could make was a large doormat, trimmed at the edges with little jingling tags like the stained porcupine quills around a Native American moccasin. There was a hole in the middle, like a South American poncho. But could any sober harpooneer actually wear a doormat through the streets of a Christian town? I tried it on. It weighed me down like a heavy basket — shaggy, thick, and I thought a little damp, as if the mysterious harpooneer had been wearing it in the rain. I went to a bit of mirror stuck on the wall. I never saw such a sight in my life. I tore myself out of it so fast I nearly wrenched my neck.

I sat on the edge of the bed, thinking about this head-peddling harpooneer and his doormat. After a while I stood up and took off my jacket, then stood in the middle of the room thinking some more. Then I took off my coat and thought further in my shirtsleeves. But starting to feel very cold, half-undressed as I was, and remembering the landlord's comment that the harpooneer might not come back at all tonight, I wasted no more time. I jumped out of my trousers and boots, blew out the light, tumbled into bed, and commended myself to heaven.

Whether that mattress was stuffed with corn cobs or broken crockery, I can't say, but I tossed and turned for a long time. At last I drifted into a light doze and had nearly reached the land of Nod when I heard a heavy footstep in the hallway and saw a glimmer of light under the door.

Lord save me, I thought — that must be the harpooneer, the infernal head-peddler. But I lay perfectly still, determined not to say a word until spoken to. Holding a light in one hand and that very New Zealand head in the other, the stranger entered the room and, without looking at the bed, placed his candle on the floor in a far corner. Then he started working at the knotted cords of the large bag I'd noticed earlier. I was desperate to see his face, but he kept it turned away while he unlaced the bag. When he finally turned around — good heavens! What a sight! Such a face! It was a dark, purplish-yellow color, covered here and there with large, blackish squares. Just as I thought — he's a terrible bedfellow; he's been in a fight, gotten horribly cut up, and just come from the surgeon. But then he turned his face toward the light, and I could plainly see those black squares weren't bandages at all. They were stains of some kind. At first I didn't know what to make of it. Then it hit me. I remembered a story about a white whaleman who'd been tattooed by cannibals. I concluded that this harpooneer, during his distant voyages, must have had a similar experience. And what of it? It's only his outside; a man can be honest in any kind of skin. But what about his unearthly complexion — the part independent of the tattoos? It might just be a heavy tropical tan, but I'd never heard of the sun turning a white man purplish-yellow. Then again, I'd never been to the South Seas. While all these thoughts were racing through my mind, the harpooneer hadn't noticed me at all. Having opened his bag, he rummaged around and pulled out a sort of tomahawk and a sealskin wallet with the fur still on. Setting these on the chest, he then took the New Zealand head — a ghastly thing — and crammed it into the bag. Then he took off his hat — a new beaver hat — and I nearly cried out in fresh surprise. There was no hair on his head to speak of — nothing but a small topknot twisted up on his forehead. His bald, purplish head looked exactly like a mildewed skull. If the stranger hadn't been standing between me and the door, I'd have bolted faster than I've ever bolted a dinner.

Even as it was, I thought something of slipping out the window, but it was the second floor at the back. I am no coward, but what to make of this head-peddling, purple-skinned rascal altogether passed my comprehension. Ignorance is the parent of fear, and being completely nonplussed and confounded about the stranger, I confess I was now as much afraid of him as if it were the devil himself who had broken into my room at the dead of night. In fact, I was so afraid of him that I wasn't game enough, just then, to address him and demand a satisfactory answer concerning what seemed inexplicable in him.

Meanwhile, he continued undressing, eventually baring his chest and arms. As I live, those parts were covered with the same dark squares as his face; his back too. He looked like he'd survived a Thirty Years' War wearing nothing but bandages. Even his legs were marked, as if dark green frogs were climbing up young palm trunks. It was now obvious: he must be some savage or other who'd shipped aboard a whaler in the South Seas and landed in this Christian country. I trembled at the thought. A peddler of heads, too — maybe even the heads of his own brothers. What if he took a fancy to mine? God — look at that tomahawk!

But there was no time for shuddering, for now the savage went about something that completely fascinated my attention and convinced me that he must indeed be a heathen. Going to his heavy grego, or wraparound, or dreadnaught coat, which he had previously hung on a chair, he fumbled in the pockets and at length produced a curious little deformed image with a hunch on its back, exactly the color of a three-day-old Congo baby. Remembering the embalmed head, at first I almost thought this black manikin was a real baby preserved in some similar manner. But seeing that it was not at all limber, and that it glistened a good deal like polished ebony, I concluded it must be nothing but a wooden idol — which indeed it proved to be. For now the savage went up to the empty fireplace, removed the papered fire-board, and set up this little hunchbacked image, like a tenpin, between the andirons. The chimney jambs and all the bricks inside were very sooty, so that I thought this fireplace made a very appropriate little shrine or chapel for his Congo idol.

I strained my eyes toward the half-hidden image, feeling very uneasy, wanting to see what came next. First he took a double handful of shavings from his coat pocket and placed them carefully before the idol. Then he laid a piece of ship biscuit on top, lit the shavings from the lamp, and kindled a little sacrificial blaze. After many hasty snatches into the fire and even hastier withdrawals of his scorched fingers, he managed to fish out the biscuit. Blowing off the heat and ashes, he politely offered it to the little figure. But the little devil didn't seem to fancy such dry fare; he never moved his lips. All these strange rituals were accompanied by still stranger guttural noises — the worshipper seemed to be praying in a singsong or chanting some pagan hymn, his face twitching in the most unnatural way. Finally, putting out the fire, he picked up the idol unceremoniously and stuffed it back in his coat pocket as casually as a hunter bagging a dead bird.

All these strange doings made me increasingly uncomfortable. Seeing that he was now showing every sign of finishing up and jumping into bed with me, I decided it was high time — now or never, before the light went out — to break the spell I'd been under.

But the moment I hesitated, deciding what to say, was fatal. Picking up his tomahawk from the table, he examined the head for a moment, then held it to his mouth by the handle and puffed out great clouds of tobacco smoke. The next instant the light went out, and this wild cannibal, tomahawk between his teeth, sprang into bed with me. I screamed — I couldn't help it. With a sudden grunt of surprise, he started feeling me all over.

Stammering out something, I knew not what, I rolled away from him against the wall, and then conjured him, whoever or whatever he might be, to keep quiet and let me get up and light the lamp again. But his guttural responses satisfied me at once that he barely understood my meaning.
'Who the devil are you?' he finally said. 'You no speak, damn me, I kill you.' And the lit tomahawk began waving around me in the dark.
'Landlord! For God's sake, Peter Coffin!' I shouted. 'Landlord! Help! Coffin! Angels! Save me!'

'Speak! Tell me who you are, or damn me, I kill you!' growled the cannibal again, his tomahawk scattering hot tobacco ashes over me until I thought my sheets would catch fire. But thank heaven, at that moment the landlord burst in with a light. I leaped from the bed and ran to him.
'Don't be afraid,' he said, grinning again. 'Queequeg here wouldn't harm a hair on your head.'
'Stop grinning!' I shouted. 'Why didn't you tell me that infernal harpooneer was a cannibal?'
'I thought you knew! Didn't I tell you he was peddling heads around town? But turn in again and go to sleep. Queequeg, look here — you understand me? This man sleep with you — you understand?'
'Me understand plenty,' grunted Queequeg, puffing away at his pipe and sitting up in bed.

'You get in,' he added, motioning to me with his tomahawk and throwing back the covers. He really did this in not only a polite but a genuinely kind and generous way. I stood looking at him for a moment. Despite all his tattoos, he was, on the whole, a clean and decent-looking cannibal. What have I been making such a fuss about? I thought. The man is a human being, just like me. He has just as much reason to fear me as I have to fear him. Better to sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

'Landlord,' I said, 'tell him to put away that tomahawk, or pipe, or whatever it is. Tell him to stop smoking — I'll share his bed. But I don't like sleeping next to a man who's smoking. It's dangerous. Besides, I'm not insured.'
When this was communicated to Queequeg, he immediately complied and politely motioned me into bed again, rolling over to one side as if to say, 'I won't touch a leg of you.'
'Good night, landlord,' I said. 'You can go.'
I turned in, and never slept better in my life.
